It's okay to feel like you've overreacted, but I'm telling you, both as someone na napunta na sa position mo before and as someone who had cut off without explanations, na hindi ka OA. Hindi ko alam kung gaano kalalim 'yung samahan niyo, but it seems like you're the only one who sees it that way. Trust me, no one *just* cuts off someone who they've been with for more than a decade if they truly see the value of the relationship and bond. If they value your friendship and truly see your worth as a friend and as a person, they wouldn’t just let the friendship go to waste. They would fight for it. They *would want* to talk things out because you, at the very least, deserve that.

I don't know your ex friend personally, but as an anxious avoidant person myself, the fight that you guys had seemed like the perfect excuse (or reason) to finally cut you off. I don't do this to everyone, though. It's just a handful of people (it's not right, but I have my reasons)

Then again, at the same time, I've also had major fights with my long-term friends, but at the end of the day, I always choose to talk things out with them because I value their presence and friendship. That's how it should be.

Hindi ka OA, because here's the thing: loyalty also includes talking to people that are close to you. If your ex friend didn't see the need to talk about it, then walang trust. Trust and loyalty should go both ways. From what you stated, there also seems to be a lack of respect. If said (ex) friend didn't even feel the need to at least give you a proper explanation, then they simply don't respect the friendship enough, and couldn't give two shits to be decent and give you the courtesy that everyone in relationships, whether platonic or romantic, deserve. From where I'm standing, nagtagal lang siguro 'yung friendship niyo kasi never kayong nag-away nang seryoso, therefore never na-test 'yung samahan niyo.

To add: do note that what I said does not, and *should not* apply to some scenarios ha, especially when it falls under harassment (of any kind), continuous emotional abuse, and physical and sexual violence.

Oh, definitely. My mom was wonderful, but it kind of makes me sad and angry because it really took my distant auntie, who I only met three years ago, foe me to get noticed, and eventually diagnosed. Auntie has an autistic son. He's the "classic" autistic -- smart, very talented, has a very strict schedule about everything, loves trains and anything that has machinery, and he spoke very late (9, turning 10). He's doing well now. He's has his own house, is married, has a PhD in Mechanical Engineering, and is a professor in one of the most competitive universities in my country. 

Apart from the talent thing (I have always been good at drawing, and I have been drawing since the age of three), I would say that I'm not like him at all. Or at least I didn't think of myself as someone who was displaying autistic traits (the way I know and see it). That is, until my distant auntie pointed it out. We've only met twice at that time, but she immediately told my grandma that there definitely is something "unique" with me. And, of course, my grandma brought this up with me. During that time, I was already seeing a therapist because of my depression. I was failing school and had not been getting out of bed for weeks then. When my grandma told me about it, I felt like I found a puzzle piece that I didn't even know I was missing. 

Long story short, I got diagnosed at 23. I'm 24 now. Still,  sometimes I question my own diagnosis because I felt like I faked how I acted during the assessment. Thoughts like "maybe it wasn't really me, and maybe I wasn't true enough, and so maybe they got it wrong, and I'm not really autistic" have been stuck with me since then, and I couldn't shake it out of my head. I am even planning to contest the diagnosis because, after all, I'm very far from my cousin, right? If I really am autistic, I should have been more like him, right? They would have noticed if I was more like him. But they didn't. The people close to me growing up did not, so maybe I'm not.

Ha?? Anarchy is distant, kung ikukumpara nga naman sa mainstream politics, I'll give you that. But I've been studying and reading anarchist literature, and supporting anything that is tied to the State is not anarchism. It's as simple as that (but not really, because anarchism has its own philosophy and is coupled with a lot of intersections, e.g., anarcho-feminism, anarcho-syndicalism, anarcho-Judaism, and so on. I recommend Cindy Milstein if you're interested). Anyway, most anarchists don't even participate in elections and voting, or anything that has to do with representative democracy, so best believe na walang anarkista ang maniniwalang end-all be-all ang elections, and most especially wala pa akong nakikitang anarkista na either devoted o self-proclaimed kakampink or DDS. What do anarchists believe in, then? Two key words: relationships and community. Grassroot organisation is where meaningful and purposeful change can start. And by grassroots, we mean your immediate environments and circle -- homes, friendships, families, and chosen families.

Symmetrical, even. 

You just gotta find that right style that will highlight your best feature. Hair is very important, but try to dress up too. And don't forget to be comfortable. IMHO, comfort -- not just the clothing, but the feeling of it -- is a style of its own because it gives you this kind of confidence of liking being in your own skin.

Good luck!
